extracted.intended_audience: general public interested in biomedical research, researchers, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria about the scientific rigor, reproducibility, and ethical/policy context of biomedical research, as discussed in a journalistic interview. Focuses on preclinical study design, replication, incentives, and communication to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility of results
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies should be reproducible; many reported findings do not stand up to replication (example: Amgen looked at 53 promising studies and could reproduce only six).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independent attempts to reproduce published studies are essential; low reproducibility even when original scientists assist indicates systemic problems. Treat single-study findings as provisional until replicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate sample size and statistical power
rubrics_metrics.description: Preclinical experiments (e.g., mouse studies) must use sufficient numbers of animals; very small sample sizes can produce misleading, non-reproducible results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments with appropriate power calculations and sample sizes to avoid false positives; avoid drawing strong conclusions from underpowered studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate consideration of model organism genetics
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers must account for the genetics and biological variability of model organisms (such as mice); failing to do so can invalidate conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully control for or characterize genetic backgrounds and other biological variables in animal studies to ensure results are generalizable and accurate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental rigor and careful laboratory practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Biomedical research requires meticulous methods and attention to experimental detail; cutting corners and 'sloppy science' reduce reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt rigorous protocols, proper controls, and consistent lab practices; guard against procedural mistakes that can lead to erroneous findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of perverse incentives (pressure to publish)
rubrics_metrics.description: Competitive funding, tenure pressures, and the drive to publish quickly can prompt scientists to cut corners and prioritize career/financial goals over scientific truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize how incentive structures influence research behavior; institutions and funders should consider reforms to reduce incentives that degrade scientific quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic motivation (focus on 'delight' and truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: A research culture that emphasizes curiosity and a commitment to truth ('delight') promotes better, more reliable science than one driven primarily by careerism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate scientific environments that reward careful, truth-seeking inquiry rather than only metrics like publication count or rapid results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and openness to replication
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers should be open about methods and willing to assist replication efforts; transparency facilitates validation and trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Share detailed methods, data, and protocols to enable others to reproduce work; openness reduces ambiguity about why results fail to replicate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent validation before clinical application
rubrics_metrics.description: Promising preclinical findings should undergo independent review and validation before being translated into human trials or clinical use (example: ALS studies later judged unrealistic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require robust, independently replicated preclinical evidence prior to initiating human trials to protect patients and avoid false hope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution in media and public communication of single studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists and the public should treat single studies as contingent; many findings will not stand the test of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overstating implications of a single paper; communicate uncertainty and the need for replication when reporting on new research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stable and sufficient funding to reduce harmful competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Cuts to research funding (e.g., NIH budget reductions) can shrink available resources and intensify competitive pressures, exacerbating perverse incentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy decisions about funding should consider effects on research quality; sufficiently stable funding pools can help mitigate rushed or sloppy science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical responsibility to patients when moving to experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Clinical enrollment of patients into experimental therapies must be justified by robust and reliable preclinical evidence; flawed earlier research can lead to unethical exposure of patients to ineffective treatments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure preclinical work is methodologically sound and replicated before exposing human subjects to interventions; protect patients from consequences of unreliable science.
